Short Description: A vast work of historical analysis that explains how Rome rose to dominate the Mediterranean world. Originally spanning 40 books, of which only the first five survive complete and the rest in fragments, it covers the period from the First Punic War to the destruction of Carthage and Corinth. Polybius, a Greek statesman from Megalopolis taken as a hostage to Rome, wrote as both participant and observer. His goal was not only to narrate events but to analyze their causes—especially the strength of Roman institutions, military discipline, and political balance. The work was composed during the decisive decades when Greece was losing its autonomy and falling under Roman control, culminating in the sack of Corinth in 146 BCE. Polybius thus writes at the threshold of a new era, interpreting Rome’s expansion for a Greek audience and bridging Hellenistic traditions of historical writing with the realities of imperial rule.

Short Description: A short pseudo-Aristotelian treatise, probably composed in the Roman period, that presents the cosmos as a unified and hierarchically ordered whole governed by a supreme divine principle. Addressed to an “Alexander,” it surveys the heavens, earth, elements, meteorological phenomena, and the structure of the inhabited world before turning to divine governance. The work draws on late Hellenistic scientific and geographical learning while remaining fundamentally Aristotelian in its theological framework. Its date is disputed, but a 1st-century CE setting is a common modern placement.

Short Description: A collection of 80 surviving discourses blending philosophy, rhetoric, civic advice, mythic reinterpretation, and political reflection. Dio was exiled under Domitian and later returned under Nerva and Trajan; his experiences of travel and exile became recurring material for moral reflection. The speeches address kingship, civic concord, freedom, virtue, and the responsibilities of Greek cities under Roman rule. Rather than simply endorsing imperial power, they repeatedly negotiate Hellenic civic identity and philosophical ideals within the political realities of the Roman Empire.

Short Description: A diverse corpus of more than 70 essays and dialogues covering ethics, religion, philosophy, politics, natural questions, education, and literary criticism. Unlike the biographical structure of the Parallel Lives, the Moralia is thematic and exploratory, ranging from practical moral advice to theological and metaphysical inquiry. Plutarch writes primarily from a Platonist perspective while engaging Stoic, Peripatetic, Pythagorean, Greek, Roman, and Egyptian traditions. The collection is therefore a major record of Greek philosophical and religious reflection within the Roman imperial world.

Short Description: This four-book medical treatise is the most comprehensive surviving ancient text on women’s medicine, pregnancy, childbirth, and infant care. Soranus systematizes earlier Hippocratic and Hellenistic medical traditions, but he also corrects and refines them with his own observations. The work covers female anatomy, conception, contraception, childbirth techniques, care for newborns, and gynecological diseases. Unlike many predecessors, Soranus emphasizes rational, empirical observation over superstition, warning against magical charms and ritual cures. He also discusses the social and ethical role of the physician and midwife, offering standards for their training and conduct.

Short Description: A collection of informal lectures by the Stoic philosopher Epictetus, transcribed by his student Arrian. Born into slavery and later freed, Epictetus turned his experience of subjugation into a lifelong commitment to philosophical freedom. Structured as practical conversations rather than systematic treatises, the Discourses focus on moral self-discipline, freedom through inner control, and alignment with divine reason (logos). Drawing from Hellenic philosophical tradition, it emphasizes that true power lies in mastering one’s judgments, not external circumstances.

Written for students and seekers, it distills the Stoic path into a portable code of life rooted in reason, resilience, and cosmic order.

Short Description: A seven-book historical account of Alexander the Great’s conquests, modeled in part on Xenophon’s Anabasis and drawing especially on the now-lost accounts of Ptolemy and Aristobulus. Arrian presents Alexander as an exceptional commander and ruler while also recording episodes of anger, excess, and deterioration in judgment. The narrative follows the campaigns from Asia Minor through the Persian Empire and India to Alexander’s death in Babylon. Written by a Greek-speaking Roman senator and governor, it frames Alexander through classical Greek historiography while remaining attentive to questions of command, kingship, discipline, and imperial power familiar to Arrian’s own age.

Lucian portrays Peregrinus as a self-dramatizing impostor and recounts his earlier association with Christians and his later Cynic career in order to mock religious credulity, philosophical pretension, and the pursuit of notoriety. Short Description: A brilliant satirical fantasy parodies the tall tales and implausible accounts of earlier historians and mythographers—especially Herodotus and Homer—by deliberately presenting an outrageous, fictional voyage as if it were fact. Lucian's narrator is swept away by a whirlwind to the Moon, where he finds warring kingdoms, strange alien creatures, and absurd customs. He later journeys inside a giant whale, discovers fantastical islands, and meets mythic figures like Homer, Pythagoras, and Odysseus in the Isle of the Blessed. The narrative is filled with playful inventions, ironic commentary, and absurd exaggerations—all the while claiming to be the only “true” account because it openly admits its falsehoods.

Short Description: A collection of Greek hexameter oracles surviving only in fragments quoted by later Platonist authors. Traditionally associated with Julian the Theurgist and, in later accounts, with his father Julian the Chaldean, the poems emerged in the late 2nd or early 3rd century CE, although their exact place of origin is unknown. They describe a transcendent paternal source, intermediary divine powers including Hecate, and ritual or theurgical means by which the soul can ascend toward the divine. Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, and other later Neoplatonists treated the Oracles as authoritative revelation, making them a major influence on late antique Platonism.

Short Description: Sextus Empiricus’s six-book skeptical attack on the learned disciplines of grammar, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, astrology, and music. He challenges claims that these fields possess secure theoretical foundations, repeatedly testing their definitions, assumptions, and standards of proof. These six books are the work strictly called Against the Professors; the separately transmitted books Against the Logicians, Against the Physicists, and Against the Ethicists belong to a related but distinct work. The aim is not to replace these disciplines with a new dogma, but to exercise Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment.

Short Description: A three-book systematic introduction to Pyrrhonian skepticism. Sextus describes the skeptical practice of setting appearances and judgments in opposition until neither side can be decisively preferred, producing suspension of judgment (epoché); tranquility (ataraxia) is presented as a consequence that can follow this suspension. The work then applies skeptical arguments to logic, physics, and ethics. Sextus does not simply prescribe disbelief in everything: the skeptic continues to live according to appearances, ordinary practices, customs, and acquired skills while withholding dogmatic assent on disputed theoretical claims.

Short Description: An eight-book biographical narrative recounting the travels, teachings, ascetic practices, wonders, and confrontations with rulers attributed to the 1st-century Pythagorean sage Apollonius of Tyana. Philostratus says the project was connected with materials supplied by Julia Domna, but the surviving work was published after her death in 217 CE, probably in the 220s or early 230s. Apollonius is presented as an ideal philosopher and holy man who travels through the Mediterranean, Mesopotamia, India, and Ethiopia, opposes tyranny, and rejects accusations of sorcery. The work blends biography, travel narrative, ethnography, miracle story, and philosophical exemplum, constructing an idealized model of Hellenic sagehood within the Roman imperial world.

Organized largely by philosophical lineage and school, it preserves material on Presocratics, Socratic traditions, the Academy, Peripatetics, Cynics, Stoics, Skeptics, and Epicureans. It remains one of the most important ancient repositories for the history and self-presentation of Greek philosophy.

Through the vine-dresser’s reports of encounters with the hero, the work retells the Trojan War, challenges parts of the Homeric tradition, and presents heroes as continuing recipients of cult who can communicate with the living. It combines literary revision of epic with descriptions of hero worship, ritual, sacred landscape, and local tradition. Within its Roman-imperial setting, the dialogue places Greek religious memory and alternative traditions about Troy at the center of cultural authority.

Short Description: The opening book of Iamblichus’s larger Pythagorean curriculum, combining a life of Pythagoras with an idealized account of the way of life attributed to his community. Pythagoras appears as a divinely favored sage, teacher, lawgiver, and founder of a disciplined philosophical tradition. The work emphasizes purification, communal life, silence, moral training, reverence for the gods, and the mathematical sciences. Rather than functioning as a modern historical biography, it uses the figure of Pythagoras to introduce and authorize Iamblichus’s late antique program of Pythagorean-Platonic education.

Short Description: An anonymous late antique compilation of Pythagorean arithmological material, traditionally attributed to Iamblichus but not regarded as the work he himself promised on the theological properties of number. Drawing heavily on Nicomachus of Gerasa and Anatolius, it interprets the numbers one through ten through divine names, mathematical properties, cosmological correspondences, and ethical symbolism. The Monad, Dyad, Triad, and the rest of the decad are treated as principles through which numerical structure can disclose features of the cosmos and the divine order. The text survives substantially and should not be described as merely fragmentary.

Short Description: A corpus of speeches and philosophical-religious compositions from Julian’s public career, including imperial panegyrics, political self-presentation, and hymnic treatments of divinity. The works reflect his development from a Christian imperial upbringing toward an explicit defense of traditional cult and Neoplatonic philosophy. Using classical rhetoric, allegorical interpretation, and Platonic cosmology, Julian reinterprets Hellenic religious and political ideals for the conditions of the 4th-century Roman Empire.

Short Description: A collection of surviving public and private correspondence attributed to Emperor Julian, ranging from administrative orders and civic matters to philosophical exchanges and religious exhortation. The letters document his relationships with officials, philosophers, priests, cities, and friends, as well as his efforts to strengthen traditional cult, reform priestly conduct, and govern after decades of Christian imperial patronage. The collection is not entirely uniform, and the authenticity of some transmitted letters has been disputed.

Short Description: A three-book polemical treatise composed at Antioch in the winter of 362–363 CE and now surviving chiefly through quotations preserved in Cyril of Alexandria’s later refutation. Julian argues that Christianity is a human construction, criticizes Christian claims about its relationship to Judaism, disputes Christian readings of Hebrew scripture, and defends traditional cults and Hellenic philosophical culture. Drawing on history, scriptural argument, and Platonic theology, the work is a major witness to pagan-Christian intellectual conflict in the 4th-century Roman Empire.

Short Description: A defense of theurgy written by Iamblichus under the persona of the Egyptian priest Abammon in response to Porphyry’s Letter to Anebo. The work argues that philosophical contemplation alone is insufficient for union with the gods and that divinely instituted rites, sacrifices, symbols, and sacred names play an essential role in the soul’s ascent. Egyptian priestly language and ritual material are central to the argument, but the treatise belongs to the Neoplatonic intellectual environment of Roman Syria rather than to an Egyptian place of composition.
